summary: Ephesians opens not with a problem but with a blessing: one long sentence praising God who blessed us, chose us, predestined us for adoption, redeemed us, and made known the mystery of his will — to sum up all things in Christ. Paul then tells the readers he never stops thanking God for their faith and love, and prays the letter's first prayer: that the eyes of their hearts be enlightened to know the hope, the inheritance, and the immeasurable power that worked when God raised Christ and seated him above every rule and authority.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the whole letter's scale: God's purpose is older than the world and larger than it, and the chapter teaches the reader where they stand inside it — in Christ, sealed with the Spirit, headed toward an inheritance. Everything the letter later asks flows from this opening doxology.

context.author: Paul, naming himself 'an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God' (1:1) — writing with the authority of a commission he did not earn.
context.audience: 'The saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus' (1:1) — believers whose faith in the Lord Jesus and love toward all the saints Paul has heard about and thanks God for (1:15).
context.date: The chapter does not date itself; it locates the reader in God's timeline instead — chosen 'before the foundation of the world' (1:4), an inheritance heading toward 'the fullness of the times' (1:10).
context.setting: A letter opening in worship rather than crisis: no opponents are named, no problems reported — the setting is the readers' standing in Christ, which the chapter blesses before it explains.
context.literaryForm: A thanksgiving letter-opening stretched into doxology: 1:3-14 runs as one long Greek sentence, chaining blessing to blessing, followed by a reported prayer (1:15-23).

outline.heading: Greeting
outline.note: Paul, apostle by God's will, to the saints and the faithful in Christ Jesus — grace and peace from the Father and the Lord.

outline.heading: The blessing: what God did in Christ
outline.note: Blessed be God, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing, chose us before the foundation, predestined us for adoption, freely gave us favor in the Beloved — to the praise of his glory.

outline.heading: Redemption, insight, and the mystery's horizon
outline.note: In him we have redemption through his blood; grace abounding in wisdom; the mystery of his will made known — an administration of fullness, to sum up all things in Christ, things in the heavens and things on the earth.

outline.heading: Inheritance, hope, and the seal
outline.note: Assigned an inheritance in him, foreordained; you heard, believed, and were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit — the pledge of the inheritance, to the praise of his glory.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving and report
outline.note: Having heard of their faith in the Lord Jesus and love toward all the saints, Paul does not cease giving thanks, making mention of them in his prayers.

outline.heading: The prayer: enlightened eyes, known power
outline.note: That the Father of glory give a spirit of wisdom and revelation; that they know the hope of his calling, the riches of the inheritance in the saints, and the exceeding greatness of his power — the power that raised Christ, seated him above every rule and authority, and made him head over all things for the assembly, his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

keyVerses.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love,
keyVerses.why: The letter's opening claim, which sets its scale: God's blessing is already given ('has blessed'), and his choice is older than the world.

keyVerses.text: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him, to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.
keyVerses.why: The mystery's content in one sentence: God's plan is to bring everything together in Christ — the widest claim the letter makes, and the reason its view stays cosmic rather than local.

keyVerses.text: which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come.
keyVerses.why: The power Paul prays they know is not abstract: it is the specific power that raised Christ and seated him above every rank — the letter's answer to every rival claim of authority.

themes: chosen and adopted before the world
summing up all things in Christ

questions.question: Why does the letter open with a blessing instead of a thanksgiving or a problem?
questions.answer: Ancient letters normally opened with a greeting and a thanksgiving; most of Paul's letters follow that pattern. Ephesians turns the opening into doxology — blessing God for what he has already done — and the shift is the signal: this letter's first move is worship, not crisis, and its claims about the reader all come as finished facts ('has blessed us,' 1:3).

questions.question: What is 'the heavenly places' in this chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase appears three times here (1:3, 1:20) and five times in the letter. In chapter 1 it is where every spiritual blessing is located (1:3) and where Christ is seated at God's right hand (1:20). It is the letter's own geography — the address of blessing, authority, and (later, 6:12) struggle — not a description of the afterlife.

questions.question: Does 'he chose us... before the foundation of the world' mean everything is decided already?
questions.answer: The chapter states the choosing plainly: God chose us in Christ before the world, predestining us for adoption (1:4-5). It is stated as praise and assurance — a purpose older than the world — and the chapter does not address how this relates to human choice. Readers and traditions differ over that relationship; the honest reading reports what the verse claims and carries the debate as a debate.

questions.question: What is the 'mystery of his will' that was made known?
questions.answer: The chapter names it: God purposed in Christ 'an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ' — things in the heavens and things on the earth (1:9-10). In this letter 'mystery' never means an unsolved riddle; it means something once hidden and now revealed. Chapter 3 will narrow it to its sharpest form: Gentiles as fellow heirs (3:6).

questions.question: What does it mean to be 'sealed with the promised Holy Spirit'?
questions.answer: The image is a seal — a mark of ownership and authenticity. The readers heard, believed, and were sealed with the Spirit, who is called 'a pledge of our inheritance' (1:13-14) — the word is an earnest, a down payment guaranteeing the whole. The Spirit is not only a present experience but the guarantee of the redemption ahead, 'to the praise of his glory.'

questions.question: What is Paul actually praying for in verses 15-23?
questions.answer: Not thanks only — a request: that God give them 'a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him' and enlighten 'the eyes of your hearts' to know three things — the hope of his calling, the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe (1:17-19). The prayer assumes they already have the things; he asks that they know them.

questions.question: Why does the prayer end by listing Christ's position — 'far above all rule, authority, power, dominion'?
questions.answer: The power Paul wants them to know is measured by what it already did: raised Christ, seated him at God's right hand, 'far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come' (1:20-21). For a congregation living under Rome, the ranking of every rival authority under Christ is both worship and quiet defiance — the letter returns to these same ranks in 6:12.

questions.question: What does 'the assembly... is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all' mean?
questions.answer: The chapter's last picture ties everything together: God made Christ 'head over all things for the assembly, which is his body' (1:22-23). The body image says connection and derivation — the assembly is Christ's own, animated by him — and 'the fullness of him who fills all in all' is one of the letter's most-pondered phrases: the filled one is also the filler. Readers take it as the assembly completing him, him filling the assembly, or both at once; the verse's plain claim is that head and body belong to a single reality.

questions.question: Why does the chapter repeat 'to the praise of his glory' three times?
questions.answer: The refrain closes each movement of the blessing (1:6, 1:12, 1:14): God's end in blessing, adopting, and sealing is not the reader's satisfaction first but his own glory. The repetition teaches the letter's posture — the reader's story exists inside a story that begins and ends in praise.

glossary.def: The letter's own phrase for where blessing is given, Christ is seated, and the struggle runs (1:3, 1:20); not a name for the afterlife.
Something once hidden and now revealed — here, God's purpose to sum up all things in Christ (1:9-10); never an unsolved puzzle in this letter.
An earnest or down payment; the Spirit is 'a pledge of our inheritance' (1:14) — the present guarantee of a future redemption.
